title: How This Library Labels Its Sources
subtitle: What Draft, Under Review, Published, Source Pending, and Verified mean — and why nothing goes live until every citation is checked
summary: The library uses editorial statuses in its CMS to manage articles and source records. Draft and Under Review identify work still being checked; Published controls public availability. Linked citation and scripture records must be verified before publication. These controls support careful review, but they are not a guarantee that every public sentence is correct, and status badges are not displayed on every article or quotation.

sections.title: Understanding How This Library Labels Its Sources
sections.body: The library uses editorial statuses in its CMS to manage articles and source records. Draft and Under Review identify work still being checked; Published controls public availability. Linked citation and scripture records must be verified before publication. These controls support careful review, but they are not a guarantee that every public sentence is correct, and status badges are not displayed on every article or quotation.

sections.title: Why a Trust System at All?
sections.body:
Religious debates often repeat verses with wrong references, misquote scholars, or copy claims without checking them. A bad argument damages trust even when offered for a true belief.

This library invites sincere investigation of Islam. Its CMS has review and source statuses to help editors track checking. Readers should still examine the linked evidence and distinguish quotations from interpretation.

sections.title: What Do the Labels Mean?
sections.body:
The CMS has article statuses and separate source statuses. Draft identifies unpublished work. Under Review identifies material prepared for editorial checking. Published makes a record available through the public library. These are workflow controls, rather than proof that every assertion has been independently established.

Linked citations and scripture records can be Source Pending or Verified. Verified should mean that an editor checked the record against its named source. It does not endorse every interpretation of that source. The publication gate blocks linked citations and scripture that are missing or remain unverified, and rejects recognized placeholder markers.

The current article and verse layouts do not display every CMS status, and there is no dedicated error-report link on every article. A correction should identify the article, the disputed wording, and the evidence supporting a change. Confirmed errors need editorial correction and renewed review; the CMS does not detect or resolve factual errors automatically.

sections.title: An Old Standard, Not a New Gimmick
sections.body:
The instinct behind these labels is ancient, and especially deep in Islamic scholarship. To separate reliable reports (hadith) of the Prophet Muhammad's words and actions (peace be upon him) from unreliable ones, Muslim scholars demanded an isnad — a stated chain of the people who transmitted each report — studied those transmitters' memory and honesty, and openly graded reports from sound to fabricated.

Christian scholarship built its own discipline, textual criticism: gathering the Bible's hand-copied manuscripts, comparing their differences, and openly printing variant readings in modern critical editions.

These editorial controls echo a valuable principle in both traditions: make sources traceable and distinguish established evidence from uncertainty.

sections.title: What the Quran Says About Verifying Information
sections.body:
The Quran addresses the handling of information directly. In Surah Al-Hujuraat, God commands:

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن جَآءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌۢ بِنَبَإٍۢ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓا۟ أَن تُصِيبُوا۟ قَوْمًۢا بِجَهَٰلَةٍۢ فَتُصْبِحُوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَٰدِمِينَ

'O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.' (Quran 49:6, Saheeh International)

The key Arabic command is fatabayyanu — investigate, make things clear before acting. This verse is the operating rule behind the Source Pending label: a quotation stays unpublished until verification is complete.

A second verse widens the principle. In Surah Al-Israa, God says:

وَلَا تَقْفُ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلْمٌ ۚ إِنَّ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْبَصَرَ وَٱلْفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْـُٔولًۭا

'And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.' (Quran 17:36, Saheeh International)

Repeating an unchecked claim is not neutral; a person is accountable before God for what they pass along. So the labels err on the side of caution: better for a true quotation to wait than for a false one to travel under our name.

sections.title: A Standard Christians Recognize Too
sections.body:
This article needs no Bible quotations, but the instinct to verify is one Christians recognize from their own scripture. Paul instructs the church in Thessalonica:

'Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.' (1 Thessalonians 5:21, World English Bible)

We quote it as an invitation: test this library by its own standard. The library uses the World English Bible, a modern public-domain translation, for its structured Bible quotations. Those quotations should be checked against the named edition before their source record is marked Verified. A reported misquotation requires correction just as an error in an Islamic source does.

sections.title: One Standard for Both Religions
sections.body:
The review standard applies to both Islamic and Christian material. Quotations should match their named sources, historical claims need evidence, and descriptions of each tradition must distinguish mainstream positions from disputed interpretations.

This library argues openly for Islam. That purpose requires presenting other beliefs accurately and correcting errors even when a mistaken claim appears to favor the Islamic argument.

sections.title: What the Labels Do Not Mean
sections.body:
'Draft means the article is wrong.' It means editorial checking is unfinished.

'Verified means the library endorses the source.' It identifies a checked source record; agreement with its doctrines is a separate question.

'Published means the article can never need correction.' Publication controls availability, and later review can still reveal mistakes.

'A status replaces evidence.' It does not. The reader can examine the named source and the reasoning that connects it to a claim.

sections.title: Verification as an Act of Faith
sections.body:
For Muslims, careful sourcing is not merely good editorial practice; it is obedience. The Quran commands believers to 'investigate' information before acting on it (Quran 49:6) and warns that a person 'will be questioned' about what they repeat (Quran 17:36). A library built to present Islam's case is therefore bound, by Islam itself, to the strictest accuracy — especially when quoting the scriptures of others.

There is a quiet argument inside the system too: a position that fears checking hides its sources, while a position confident of the truth invites scrutiny.

Read the linked sources, check important quotations, and approach unfinished evidence with caution. A confirmed error should be corrected and reviewed. Careful scrutiny serves the truth and the Islamic duty to speak with knowledge.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: How This Library Labels Its Sources
sections.body: Reliable investigation of Islam requires primary texts and honest acknowledgment of uncertainty. The CMS's publication and source controls support that work, but cannot replace editorial judgment or prove that every claim is correct. Islam's invitation is strongest when its evidence is open to checking and mistakes are corrected.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: What is the difference between Draft and Under Review?
A: Both are unpublished editorial states. Draft is unfinished work; Under Review identifies material being prepared or checked.

Q: What does Verified mean for a scripture record?
A: It should mean that an editor checked the quotation against its named edition. It does not endorse every interpretation.

Q: Can a Published article need correction?
A: Yes. Editors can correct it and return it to review when needed.

Q: Does every article have an error-report button?
A: No. The current layouts do not provide a dedicated error-report link on every article. A useful correction identifies the article, the disputed wording, and a supporting source.

Q: What does the publication gate check?
A: It blocks missing or unverified linked source records and recognized placeholders. It cannot determine whether every historical or theological claim is true.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World** — Jonathan A. C. Brown. An accessible academic introduction to how Muslim scholars authenticated reports about the Prophet, including chains of transmission and narrator criticism — the historical ancestor of source-verification systems like this library's.
- **Studies in Hadith Methodology and Literature** — Muhammad Mustafa al-Azami. A concise Muslim scholar's account of the classical methods used to grade reports as sound, weak, or fabricated.
- **The Text of the New Testament: Its Transmission, Corruption, and Restoration** — Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman. The standard introduction to Christian textual criticism — how scholars compare biblical manuscripts and rate the confidence behind different readings.

faq.question: What is the difference between Draft and Under Review?
faq.answer: Both are unpublished editorial states. Draft is unfinished work; Under Review identifies material being prepared or checked. The status alone does not tell a reader which individual claims have been checked.

faq.question: What does Verified mean for a scripture quotation?
faq.answer: It was compared word-for-word against a named edition — the Tanzil Uthmani Arabic text with the Saheeh International translation for Quran verses, and the World English Bible for Bible verses. Verified is a claim about accurate quotation, not endorsement of any interpretation of the verse.

faq.question: Can a Published article lose its Published status?
faq.answer: Yes. Editors can return an article to review and correct it when an error is confirmed. This requires editorial action; publication is not a permanent guarantee of correctness.

faq.question: Does every article have an error-report button?
faq.answer: No. The current layouts do not provide a dedicated error-report link on every article. A useful correction identifies the article, the disputed wording, and a supporting source.

faq.question: What does the publication gate check?
faq.answer: It blocks missing or unverified linked citation and scripture records and recognized placeholder markers. This protects source integrity, but does not automatically decide whether every historical, scientific, or theological claim is true.
